01 The Hook

Fewer bike rides on cold days?

On days officials label "Bad" air quality, Seoul's bike-share rentals look lower — a simple regression of Bad days vs. every other day finds:

Guess first

15% fewer

Choose 0–30%, then lock it in to compare with the data below.

0.0%
Bad day (PM2.5 >35 µg/m³) vs. all other days · log-OLS, HAC standard errors · 95% CI −21.1% to +1.6% · p=0.086 · 727 days (2024–2025)

Poor air quality is often assumed to discourage cycling. In Seoul, bike rentals initially appear 10.5% lower on "Bad" PM2.5 days, but does pollution itself explain this difference, or do weather and seasonal conditions play a larger role? Our investigation examines whether the apparent relationship remains after accounting for these overlapping factors.

02 The Investigation

Han River classification

We classified every Seoul bike-share station by straight-line distance to the Han River water boundary using station coordinates: 159 stations fall within 500 m, 405 stations within 1 km, out of 2,904 stations citywide.

Han River Within 500 m Other stations

Hover a dot for station name and distance to the Han River. River boundary © OpenStreetMap contributors.

Round-trip definition

A round trip returns to the same station it was rented from, excluding trips of 2 minutes or less (to drop accidental re-docks). Round trips are used as a proxy for leisure/exercise riding vs. point-to-point commuting.

A note on two different "raw gap" numbers. You may also see −11.3% quoted elsewhere: that's a Welch one-sided t-test comparing the average rentals on Good days (108,623) vs. Bad days (96,359) directly (t=2.20, p=0.015). The −10.5% headline above is a log-OLS regression of Bad-day status against every other day. They compare slightly different things (simple average gap vs. regression coefficient), so they aren't expected to match exactly — we use the regression number as the primary headline, consistent with our Week 5 report.

05 The Evidence

Double Machine Learning (DML) results: random forests flexibly absorb weather/calendar/season/trend, then we read off what's left of the PM2.5 relationship. Solid marker = 95% CI excludes zero; hollow/dashed = not significant.

The workday Han River result was not pre-specified and is exploratory: a relative-share change only. Absolute Han River rentals are not significant. Day-off estimates are similar in size but imprecise, with no clear response.

06 What the Data Shows

Carbon scenario · What if bike kilometres were lost?

Scenario based on assumptions, not a measurement. Our data show no meaningful ride loss.

Default ≈5,200 km/day: the approximate 2% upper bound applied to about 259,000 bike km/day (727-day mean). Slider spans zero to that daily distance; every setting is hypothetical.

Replaced by car:
Assumed added car emissions · kgCO₂eq/day

Passenger-car factor: 0.2111 kgCO₂eq/passenger-km · Ministry of Environment & Korea Environment Corporation, 2024. Assumes each replaced bike kilometre becomes one passenger-kilometre by car.

0.232 kg/km is Seoul's own carbon-saving coefficient in the raw rental data. This scenario uses the separate passenger-car factor above.

From Air Quality to Carbon Emissions

The analysis above finds that the city-wide PM2.5 effect on daily Ttareungyi rentals is close to zero after controlling for weather, season, calendar, and trend. That does not establish that poor air quality causes people to stop cycling or switch to cars. The following is therefore a what-if scenario: if cycling distance falls and some of that distance is replaced by passenger-car travel, additional transport emissions could result.

How this connects to our findings: Map A shows that temperature and other contextual factors are more strongly associated with daily rentals than PM2.5 alone. Map B illustrates how season and weather can confound the apparent relationship. The DML results likewise do not support a clear city-wide causal effect of PM2.5 on rentals. The carbon estimates should therefore be read as conditional scenarios—not measured emissions or evidence that PM2.5 actually causes a shift to cars.

Policy implication: During periods of poor air quality, reliable public transport and other low-emission travel options can help reduce emissions if people avoid cycling. The scenario values are illustrative and depend on the stated assumptions.

Source: Carbon Emission Scenarios: Switching from Ttareungyi (Public Bike-Sharing) to Passenger Cars, based on the 2024 Ministry of Environment & Korea Environment Corporation emission-factor guideline. Passenger-car emission intensity: 0.2111 kgCO₂eq/passenger-km.

Our findings suggest that weather, seasonal patterns, and calendar factors are important for understanding daily bike-sharing demand. Although PM2.5 showed no statistically significant association with overall rentals after adjustment, the exploratory Han River result suggests that certain usage patterns may respond differently (not pre-specified; a relative-share change only). These findings highlight the importance of considering contextual factors rather than interpreting pollution levels in isolation. Our pre-specified hypothesis that leisure riders on days off react more was not supported.

Seoul's bike-sharing policies should consider weather conditions, seasonal demand, and air quality when planning services. During periods of poor air quality, providing reliable public transportation and other low-emission alternatives may help prevent a shift toward private cars if riders do avoid cycling on such days.

07 Exploratory Patterns

Raw (pre-control) averages by PM2.5 grade and day type — these describe the data, they are not causal estimates.

Workday Day off

Han River 500m share

Round-trip share

Across all PM2.5 categories, trips on days off were generally longer in both duration and distance than trips on workdays. Commuter-pass usage was more prevalent on workdays, while age-group distributions remained relatively stable across air-quality categories. These descriptive patterns suggest that travel purpose and day type may help explain differences in bike-sharing behavior, although they do not establish causal effects.

08 Three System Maps

Map A — Statistical significance (regression)

Each variable regressed alone on log(rentals); arrow thickness = R² (R² values overlap, so don't add them). Temperature explains the most alone (R²=31.2%, p<0.001); PM2.5 alone explains almost nothing (R²=0.04%, p=0.686).

Map B — Theory / scenario-based

Map B illustrates how seasonal and weather conditions may influence both PM2.5 concentrations and bike-sharing demand, creating potential confounding relationships. For example, colder seasonal conditions may coincide with higher pollution and lower cycling activity, making the direct effect of PM2.5 appear stronger than it is. Nonlinear (threshold) and delayed responses shown on the map were tested and not supported.

Map C — Machine Learning (Double ML)

Random forests explain 85% of day-to-day variation in rentals and 42% of PM2.5 variation out-of-fold. Once removed: city-wide effect −0.32% (CI −1.83 to +1.21, n.s.); Han River share, workdays, −1.17% (CI −1.75 to −0.58, p<0.001).

The workday Han River result was not pre-specified and is exploratory, a relative-share change only. Absolute Han River rentals are not significant.

09 Limitations & Future Work

How we kept ourselves honest

  • Rules fixed in advance: 500 m and 1 km station cutoffs, the same-station round-trip rule excluding trips of 2 minutes or less, and robustness checks. The workday Han River result was not pre-specified and remains exploratory: a relative-share change only; absolute Han River rentals are not significant.
  • Rainfall blanks: treated as no rain after checking KMA's handling; this matches KMA's 227 rain days.
  • Excluded days: 731 days minus 3 days with missing wind and 2025-02-28 leaves 727 analysis days. Very Bad (1 day) is merged into Bad.
  • Serial dependence: Newey-West standard errors account for autocorrelation.
  • Cross-fitting: DML uses 5-fold cross-fitting over 5 seeds; results summarize the median across seeds.

Limits of the evidence

  • Only 18 day-off "Bad" days in the sample — day-off-specific estimates (e.g. the leisure-rider test) rest on a small subsample and have wide confidence intervals.
  • No hourly data: we can't separate rush-hour commute trips from leisure trips within a day, only daily totals.
  • Only 7 days with a PM10 advisory in effect in the sample — too few to study alert-level pollution separately from ordinary "Bad" days.
  • Han River–specific events or closures (festivals, path closures, flooding) are not controlled for.
  • The workday Han River share result (−1.1% to −1.2%) was not pre-specified before analysis and is a relative-share change only — absolute Han River rentals (ln_h500) are not significant, so treat this as exploratory rather than confirmatory.
  • Two "raw gap" numbers (Welch −11.3% vs. regression −10.5%) compare slightly different things; we standardize on the regression number throughout.
  • Seoul's carbon-saving coefficient in the raw rental data is 0.232 kg/km. Car-replacement scenarios use the separate 2024 passenger-car factor and are assumptions, not measurements; our data show no meaningful ride loss.
  • Adding sunshine/cloud controls drops the usable sample to 725 days (239 days off) — two extra days were excluded for missing sunshine data.
  • Time-ordered (non-shuffled) cross-fitting folds give noisier, sometimes different estimates than random folds — a caution on fold design, not a contradiction.
  • Our Week 4 notebook settings reproduce as −0.32% city-wide (vs. −0.315% originally reported); the small difference reflects a v2→v3 data update.

This project demonstrates the importance of moving beyond simple correlations in data-driven decision-making. By progressively incorporating regression controls and machine learning, we learned how confounding factors can change the interpretation of an apparent relationship. Future research could incorporate hourly usage data, individual travel decisions, and actual transportation substitution patterns to better understand behavioral responses to air pollution.
